title: Zeal in amending (I.25)
hook: keep watch over yourself with steady zeal
tomorrow: is the kingdom of God a place you can point to?

segments.voice: Yesterday: order each act and thought as if this were the last day, with a clear conscience instead of fear. The line was as if today.

January resolutions burn hot. Some of them are cold by February. Big promises often go that way: a burst, a slip, then quiet. The Imitation tells a story about a man who wanted a guarantee before he'd fully commit. He knelt before an altar, worn out with worry, and said: if only I knew that I would persevere! Then, the book says, he heard an answer inside him. It wasn't a guarantee. It was a question.
screen: `HOT IN JANUARY, COLD BY FEBRUARY.` → `IF ONLY I KNEW I'D PERSEVERE.` → `THE ANSWER WAS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: What would you do if you knew? Do now what you'd do then, and you'll be secure. That's the answer the man heard, and the book says his anxious wavering stopped. He quit prying into the future and looked for what God wanted, to begin and finish each good work. That's the Imitation's zeal: not a bonfire, a watch. Keep watch over yourself, chapter twenty-five says, stir yourself up, warn yourself, and whatever happens to others, don't neglect yourself. What bothers you in someone else, avoid in yourself. Steady, not loud. The book even admits the cost: you'll make progress, it says, in proportion to the effort you put into yourself. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, Max Müller's translation reads: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm." Both picture change as watchfulness kept up day after day, not one heroic vow. Both put the work close to home: yourself first, not your neighbor. And here's an honest difference. The man in the Imitation finds his peace by handing the future to God's will and asking grace to begin. The Dhammapada's verse names no God to lean on; the rousing and the island are the wise person's own. Two old answers to the same January question, each in its own words.
screen: `DO NOW WHAT YOU'D DO THEN.` · `NOT A BONFIRE, A WATCH.` · `AN ISLAND NO FLOOD CAN OVERWHELM.` · `ONE HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `STEADY ZEAL.`

segments.voice: Choose one small habit you'd like to amend. Name what you want, then the obstacle that usually trips you, then one plan: when that moment comes, I'll do this instead. Keep it small enough to start today. Hold the plan quietly for the sit, and if you pray, place it in God's hands.
Zeal in amending. The Imitation's counsel: keep watch over yourself, and set your life right steadily, one good work at a time, starting now.
Your line: steady zeal. A watch kept every day outlasts a vow shouted once. That's today.

notes: Imitation I.25 paraphrased: be watchful and diligent and often consider why you came; the story of one anxious, wavering between fear and hope, who prostrated himself in prayer before an altar and said 'O if I knew that I should persevere', and heard within 'What wouldst thou do if thou knewest it? Do now what thou wouldst then do, and thou shalt be secure'; comforted, he committed himself to God's will, his anxious wavering ceased, and he sought God's will for beginning and finishing every good work; what displeases you in others, avoid in yourself; watch over thyself, stir up thyself, admonish thyself, and whatever becomes of others, neglect not thyself.
